prompt: In the lesson's connection diagram (Digitakt, DIY synth, USB audio interface, computer running Ableton), which device is the USB host?

options.text: The Digitakt
options.explanation: The Digitakt's USB-B port is for connecting to a computer host; it acts as a USB device.

options.text: The audio interface
options.explanation: A USB audio interface is a device that the computer hosts.

options.text: The DIY synth
options.explanation: Unless you build it with a USB host port and host firmware, a dev board's USB is a device port.

options.text: The computer
options.explanation: Correct. The computer hosts the interface (and the Digitakt if its USB is connected). The Digitakt-to-synth link uses DIN MIDI, which needs no host.

workedExample:
List each USB connection and its roles:

```
interface USB  -> computer (host)
Digitakt USB   -> computer (host)
Digitakt->synth: DIN MIDI, no USB
```

Every USB link has exactly one host, and in this design it's always the computer. That is why the Digitakt can drive the synth even with the computer switched off.

prompt: You connect the Digitakt's MIDI OUT to your synth, but the synth receives nothing. A MIDI monitor on that cable shows no messages, yet an oscilloscope shows regular pulses on the line while the Digitakt plays. Which setting should you check first?

options.text: USB CONFIG: set it to OVERBRIDGE
options.explanation: USB configuration doesn't affect what the DIN MIDI OUT port sends.

options.text: SETTINGS > MIDI CONFIG > PORT CONFIG > OUT PORT FUNC: set it to MIDI, not DIN 24 or DIN 48
options.explanation: Correct. In DIN sync modes the port sends sync pulses and no MIDI data.

options.text: The track's VEL parameter
options.explanation: Velocity affects notes, but the problem here is that the port isn't sending MIDI at all.

options.text: CLOCK RECEIVE
options.explanation: That controls whether the Digitakt follows incoming clock; it doesn't change what MIDI OUT sends.

workedExample:
1. Both Digitakt manuals: the MIDI OUT/SYNC A port can send MIDI, DIN 24 or DIN 48 sync. In the DIN sync modes, "No MIDI data is transferred over the port".
2. Pulses that don't decode as MIDI suggest sync mode.
3. Set OUT PORT FUNC to MIDI and OUTPUT TO to MIDI (or MIDI+USB), as in the manuals' "Controlling a synthesizer" procedure.
4. Then set CHAN on the track's SRC page to the synth's channel.

prompt: Which statements about Digitakt MIDI tracks match Elektron's manuals? Select all that apply.

options.text: On the original Digitakt, tracks 9–16 are dedicated MIDI tracks
options.explanation: Correct. The original has eight dedicated MIDI tracks (TRK 9–16).

options.text: On the Digitakt II, any of the 16 tracks can be a MIDI track once the MIDI machine is assigned to it
options.explanation: Correct, per the Digitakt II manual.

options.text: On both, a MIDI track's channel is set with CHAN on its SRC page
options.explanation: Correct. CHAN ranges over OFF and 1–16 and can't be parameter-locked.

options.text: MIDI tracks on both models send audio as well as MIDI
options.explanation: MIDI tracks generate no sound; their data goes out of MIDI OUT or USB.

options.text: The Digitakt II offers only 8 assignable CCs per MIDI track
options.explanation: The Digitakt II has 16 assignable CCs per MIDI track; the original has 8.

workedExample:
From the manuals checked on 4 October 2026:

```
          Digitakt     Digitakt II
MIDI trks 9-16 fixed   any of 16
CCs/track 8            16
channel   SRC > CHAN   SRC > CHAN
```

Confirm against your own model's current manual: menus and limits can change between OS versions.

prompt: A Digitakt MIDI trig has NOT2–NOT4 set, so it sends a four-note chord to your mono synth using last-note priority. What will you hear?

options.text: One note: whichever of the four Note On messages arrived last
options.explanation: Correct. The note stack receives all four; last-note priority sounds the most recent. The order depends on how the Digitakt sends them.

options.text: A four-note chord
options.explanation: A mono synth has one voice, so it can't play all four notes.

options.text: Silence, because the synth can't handle chords
options.explanation: Note priority handles multiple held notes; it picks one.

options.text: The lowest note, always
options.explanation: That would be low-note priority.

workedExample:
1. Four Note On messages arrive in quick succession (on DIN, about 1 ms apart).
2. The synth's note stack holds all four.
3. Last-note priority picks the most recently received one.
4. Because they arrive almost together, you may hear a very brief blip of the earlier notes, depending on your envelope and retrigger behaviour.

For a mono synth, leave NOT2–NOT4 at 0 unless you want this effect.

prompt: Ableton runs at 48 kHz with a 256-sample buffer. Ignoring converter delays, what is the minimum extra delay when you monitor the synth *through* Ableton (one input buffer plus one output buffer)?

options.text: About 2.7 ms
options.explanation: That is a single 128-sample buffer at 48 kHz.

options.text: About 5.3 ms
options.explanation: That is one 256-sample buffer. Monitoring through software needs at least an input buffer and an output buffer.

options.text: About 0.5 ms
options.explanation: Far too short for a 256-sample buffer at this sample rate.

options.text: About 10.7 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 256 / 48,000 = 5.33 ms per buffer, × 2 ≈ 10.7 ms, before converter and driver delays are added.

workedExample:
```
one buffer = 256 / 48000
           = 5.33 ms
in + out   = 2 * 5.33 = 10.67 ms
```

Real round-trip latency is higher (converters, driver safety buffers). If it feels late, monitor directly on the interface and set the Live track's monitor to Off, or reduce the buffer size.

link.title: Live 12 manual: Routing and I/O — Ableton

prompt: Playing the synth from the Digitakt while monitoring through an armed Ableton track (monitor: Auto) feels sluggish. What is the best change for tracking?

options.text: Raise Ableton's buffer size
options.explanation: A larger buffer increases the monitoring delay.

options.text: Use the interface's direct monitoring and set the track's monitor to Off
options.explanation: Correct. Direct monitoring routes the input to the outputs inside the interface, bypassing the computer's buffers. Live's manual mentions this use of Off.

options.text: Switch the Digitakt to USB MIDI
options.explanation: The delay is in the audio monitoring path, not in the Digitakt's MIDI.

options.text: Increase the interface input gain
options.explanation: Level has nothing to do with timing.

workedExample:
1. The sluggish feel comes from audio round-trip latency through Live.
2. Direct monitoring in the interface has almost no delay.
3. Turning Live's track monitor Off avoids hearing the signal twice (direct plus delayed).
4. Recording timing is handled separately by Live's latency settings, and should be checked with a loopback/timing test; driver reporting and monitoring options affect alignment.

link.title: Live 12 manual: Routing and I/O — Ableton

prompt: You want the Digitakt and Ableton to stay in time. Which clock arrangement is sound?

options.text: Digitakt CLOCK SEND on; Live set to follow the Digitakt as an external sync source (EXT on)
options.explanation: Correct. One master (the Digitakt), one follower (Live). The reverse (Live master, Digitakt CLOCK RECEIVE on) is equally valid.

options.text: Enable CLOCK SEND on the Digitakt and also make Live send clock to the Digitakt
options.explanation: Two clock sources talking to each other give conflicting tempos. Choose a single master.

options.text: No clock: just press play on both at the same moment
options.explanation: Two independent clocks drift apart, and the start will never be sample-accurate.

options.text: Use MIDI Timecode from the Digitakt
options.explanation: The Digitakt manuals describe MIDI clock and transport for sync. Live's manual also notes timecode carries no tempo, so it can't follow tempo changes.

workedExample:
1. MIDI clock is 24 `F8` per quarter note from one master.
2. Digitakt: SETTINGS > MIDI CONFIG > SYNC has CLOCK SEND/RECEIVE and TRANSPORT SEND/RECEIVE.
3. Live: enable the Digitakt as a sync source in Tempo & MIDI settings, then switch on EXT; Live can be a MIDI clock host or follower.
4. Pick one direction and disable the other to avoid conflicting tempo sources.

link.title: Live 12 manual: Synchronizing with Link, Tempo Follower and MIDI — Ableton

prompt: During development your dev-board synth is powered by USB from the laptop, and its audio output goes into the USB interface on the same laptop. You hear a steady hum that disappears when you unplug the synth's USB cable. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A MIDI fault on the DIN cable
options.explanation: DIN MIDI is optically isolated and carries no audio-frequency ground current; and the hum tracks the USB cable.

options.text: The synth's sample rate doesn't match the interface's
options.explanation: Sample-rate mismatches don't arise across an analogue audio cable, and they don't sound like steady hum.

options.text: A ground loop: the synth's ground connects to the laptop through USB and also to the interface through the audio cable shield
options.explanation: Correct. Two ground paths between the same devices form a loop, and current in the shared ground appears as hum.

options.text: Phantom power is turned on
options.explanation: Phantom power is a DC supply on mic inputs; it doesn't cause hum that tracks a USB cable.

workedExample:
1. USB connects host and device grounds.
2. The synth's ground therefore meets the laptop's ground twice: via its own USB cable, and via the audio shield → interface → interface USB → laptop.
3. That loop lets current flow in the audio ground, which is heard as hum.
4. Unplugging one path (the synth's USB) breaks the loop, supporting the diagnosis; a changed power supply can also change supply noise.
5. Fixes: a different power source plus DIN MIDI, a USB isolator, a balanced connection, or an audio isolation transformer.

prompt: Which are **safe** ways to deal with a ground-loop hum in this studio? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use balanced TRS connections into the interface's balanced line inputs
options.explanation: Correct. A differential input rejects much of the ground noise as common mode.

options.text: Insert a ground loop isolation transformer in the affected audio line
options.explanation: Correct. It passes the signal and breaks the DC ground path.

options.text: Remove the earth pin connection from a mains-powered device
options.explanation: Never. That removes protection against electric shock; the ground loop must be fixed on the signal side.

options.text: Connect devices with DIN MIDI rather than USB where possible
options.explanation: Correct. DIN MIDI inputs are optically isolated; USB joins grounds.

options.text: Make the audio cables as long as possible
options.explanation: Longer cables pick up more interference and add resistance to the ground path; keep them short.

workedExample:
Work from safe, signal-side fixes:

1. Balanced connections: common-mode rejection.
2. Isolation transformer: breaks the ground path in one audio line.
3. DIN MIDI instead of USB: removes a ground path.
4. Never defeat a mains safety earth.

Diagnose first by unplugging one connection at a time.

prompt: Your Digitakt II can output up to +18 dBu peak. Suppose your interface's line input accepts a maximum of +10 dBu. How far over could the Digitakt drive it, and what should you do?

options.text: 2 dB over; ignore it
options.explanation: 18 − 10 = 8 dB, not 2. And clipping at the input can't be fixed later in Ableton.

options.text: No problem, because dBu levels can't clip
options.explanation: Every input has a maximum level; exceeding it clips.

options.text: Raise Ableton's track fader to compensate
options.explanation: The overload happens at the interface's input stage, before Ableton sees the audio.

options.text: 8 dB over; lower the Digitakt's output level or use the interface's pad/line setting until peaks stay below the input's maximum
options.explanation: Correct. Both figures are in dBu, so you can subtract: 18 − 10 = 8 dB of possible overload.

workedExample:
1. Both levels use the same reference (dBu), so subtract: 18 − 10 = 8 dB.
2. 8 dB is about 2.5× in voltage: peaks well beyond what the input accepts.
3. Clipping at the converter is permanent in the recording.
4. Reduce the source (Digitakt master level) or the input's sensitivity (pad, line/instrument switch), then set gain so peaks leave headroom.

(The +10 dBu figure is hypothetical; read your own interface's specification.)

prompt: One note in a Digitakt MIDI track pattern keeps sounding on your synth long after the others have ended, but your parser passes all its unit tests. What is the first thing to check on the Digitakt?

options.text: The Digitakt's sample rate
options.explanation: The Digitakt's audio sample rate has nothing to do with MIDI note lengths.

options.text: The trig's LEN, which the original Digitakt manual says can be set to INF (infinite note length)
options.explanation: Correct. An infinite length holds the note by design, so the synth is doing what it was told.

options.text: The FX CONTROL CH setting
options.explanation: That channel concerns the Digitakt's own effects parameters, not note lengths on a MIDI track.

options.text: The headphone level
options.explanation: Audio monitoring level doesn't affect when MIDI note offs are sent.

workedExample:
1. Separate sender problems from receiver problems: monitor the MIDI and see whether a note off is ever sent.
2. On a Digitakt MIDI track, LEN decides when the note off goes out. The original manual lists LEN values up to 128 and an INF setting for infinite note length.
3. If no note off is sent, the synth is right to keep playing.
4. If a note off *is* sent and the synth ignores it, look at your channel handling and velocity-0 normalisation.

prompt: You let Ableton play the synth through the External Instrument device. Recorded notes consistently land about 3 ms late compared with Live's own instruments. Where is this compensated?

options.text: Increase the audio buffer size
options.explanation: That increases latency; it doesn't compensate for the hardware delay.

options.text: Change the MIDI channel
options.explanation: Channel selection doesn't affect timing.

options.text: The External Instrument device's Hardware Latency slider
options.explanation: Correct. Live can't detect the delay through external hardware automatically; you set it here, in milliseconds or samples.

options.text: Turn on the Digitakt's CLOCK SEND
options.explanation: Clock sync aligns tempo between sequencers; it doesn't remove the delay through your synth and interface.

workedExample:
1. Live's manual: external devices can introduce latency that Live cannot detect automatically, so the External Instrument device has a Hardware Latency slider.
2. Measure the offset: record your synth and a Live instrument triggered on the same beat, and compare the waveforms in samples.
3. Enter it (3 ms ≈ 144 samples at 48 kHz). The manual suggests samples for digital connections, so the value holds if the sample rate changes.
4. The slider is disabled if Delay Compensation is turned off in the Options menu.

link.title: Live 12 manual: Live Instrument Reference (External Instrument) — Ableton
